This scenario analyzed four field lighting measures, including average horizontal illuminance, minimum horizontal illuminance, maximum horizontal illuminance, and horizontal illuminance variance. The scenario included the following analyses: ND crash ratios (nighttime after 8:00 p.m.) on local roadways. This o analysis involved the development of four linear mixed-effect models for 68 the four lighting measures respectively. However, none of the lighting measures were found significant. Nighttime crashes (after 10:00 p.m.) on C2 roadways for Cambridge and o HPMS roadways for Somerville. This analysis included four mixed-effect negative binomial regression models by lighting measures comparing nighttime crash frequencies at different light conditions during nighttime. The results similarly showed that none of the four lighting measures analyzed were significant. Nighttime crashes (after midnight) on C1 roadways for Cambridge and o HPMS roadways for Somerville. Similarly, the research team attempted to develop mixed-effect negative binomial regression models for the four lighting measures but none of the models were able to be optimized. Due to this reason, the project team developed fixed-effect negative binomial regression models instead. Among the four models, the results showed that average illuminance and illuminance variance were significant. The following summarizes the findings of this comprehensive analysis: • For all nighttime crashes, the analysis showed that the two cities did not have statistically significantly different nighttime crashes after the LED system was implemented when controlling other variables. Both of the daytime models, however, showed that the Cambridge Indicator variable was significant, with the after LED conversion model being considerably higher than that of the before LED conversion model, indicating Cambridge had higher daytime crashes after the LED implementation. Taking into consideration the daytime models, the results potentially indicated that the LED system at Cambridge functioned well in reducing the higher nighttime crash frequencies in the city to similar levels compared to Somerville. • When analyzing the roadways by dimming schedule, the results showed that the adaptive system had negligible or no effects on ND crash ratios for local roads. The analysis for C2 roadways after 10:00 p.m. also showed that the adaptive lighting system was not a significant factor for nighttime crashes. The analysis for C1 roadways and nighttime crashes after midnight, however, seemingly suggested higher nighttime crash frequencies after midnight with the adaptive system. This result, however, needs to be viewed in the context of very few nighttime crashes during this period and minor injury and property damage only crashes being the dominant crash types. • When analyzing nighttime crashes by lighting levels, the results showed that none of the lighting measures were significant for local roads after 8:00 p.m. and C2 roadways after 10:00 p.m.. However, for the after midnight crash analysis on C1 roadways, the results showed that each increase of 1 lux in average illuminance correlated with an approximate 1.7% reduction in nighttime crash frequency.
